hmmt-nov-2025-thm-01.title: Track the mercury
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-01.body:
Pouring mixture out of $B$ does not change its concentration, so $B$ was $30\%$ mercury (and $70\%$ gallium) when it was full. A full $B$ holds $1$ liter, so exactly $0.3$ L of mercury was poured into it from $A$.

Then $0.3$ L of the $30\%/70\%$ mixture is poured back into $A$ to fill it up again; this contains $0.3\cdot0.7=0.21$ L of gallium. Flask $A$ now holds $0.21$ L of gallium and $0.79$ L of mercury, so $x=79$.

**Answer: 79**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-02.title: Venn diagram
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-02.body:
Every moon has at least one of the three properties. A moon outside the three groups "blue but not icy", "icy but not large", "large but not blue" must have all three properties: if it is blue it must be icy, if icy it must be large, if large it must be blue, and it has at least one property. Conversely a moon with all three properties is in none of the groups.

So the moons that are blue, icy and large are exactly those outside the three (disjoint) groups, and their number is $29-10-8-6=5$.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-03.title: Parallel lines give equal areas
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-03.body:
Since $SE\parallel UN$, triangles $SUN$ and $EUN$ have the same base $UN$ and the same height, so $[EUN]=[SUN]=24$. Since $NV\parallel SU$, triangles $SUN$ and $SUV$ have the same base $SU$ and the same height, so $[SUV]=[SUN]=24$.

The pentagon $VENUS$ is split into $\triangle EUN$, $\triangle SUV$ and $\triangle EUV$, hence
$$[EUV]=84-24-24=36.$$
The value is forced, so the maximum is $36$.

**Answer: 36**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-04.title: Column by column
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-04.body:
Add the two numbers $\underline{HATER}+\underline{HEART}=\underline{EARTH}$.

*Thousands column.* The digits added are $A$ and $E$, and the result digit is $A$, so $E+(\text{carry})\equiv 0\pmod{10}$, which forces $E=0$ or $E=9$. $E$ is a leading digit, so $E=9$ (and a carry of $1$ comes in).

*Ten-thousands column.* $H+H+1=E=9$ (there is no carry out because the sum has five digits), so $H=4$.

*Ones column.* $R+T\equiv H=4\pmod{10}$, so $R+T=4$ or $14$.

*Tens column.* $E+R+c\equiv T$, where $c$ is the carry from the ones column; with $E=9$ this reads $R+c\equiv T+1\pmod{10}$. If $R+T=4$ (so $c=0$) we get $R\equiv T+1$, which gives $2T+1=4$, impossible. If $R+T=14$ ($c=1$) we get $R\equiv T$, so $R=T=7$.

*Hundreds column.* $T+A+1\equiv R$ (a carry of $1$ comes from the tens column since $9+7+1=17$), i.e. $A+1\equiv0$, so $A=9$.

So $\underline{EARTH}=99774$. Check: $49797+49977=99774$.

**Answer: 99774**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-05.title: Stars and bars
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-05.body:
The string has $30$ letters. The $4$ kept letters cut the $26$ erased letters into five (possibly empty) blocks: before the first kept letter, between consecutive kept letters, and after the last.

Number the letters $1,\dots,30$; position $i$ holds S, U, N when $i\equiv1,2,0\pmod 3$. The kept positions $p_1<p_2<p_3<p_4$ must satisfy $p_1\equiv1$, $p_2\equiv2$, $p_3\equiv0$, $p_4\equiv1\pmod3$. The block lengths are $p_1-1$, $p_2-p_1-1$, $p_3-p_2-1$, $p_4-p_3-1$, which are all $\equiv0\pmod3$, and $30-p_4\equiv2\pmod 3$.

Write the block lengths as $3a_0,3a_1,3a_2,3a_3,3a_4+2$ with $a_i\ge0$. Their sum is $26$, so $3(a_0+\dots+a_4)+2=26$ and $a_0+\dots+a_4=8$. By stars and bars the number of solutions is $\binom{8+4}{4}=\binom{12}{4}=495$. Each solution gives exactly one way of choosing the erased positions.

**Answer: 495**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-06.title: Annulus sector plus half hexagons
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-06.body:
$ST$ is a short diagonal of the hexagon, so $ST=2\sqrt3$. As $O$ is the reflection of $T$ over $S$, $OS=ST=2\sqrt3$ and $OT=4\sqrt3$. Also $\angle OTU=\angle STU=120^\circ-30^\circ=90^\circ$, so $OU^2=OT^2+TU^2=48+4=52$ and $OS^2=12$.

Among the points of the hexagon, $S$ is the closest to $O$ and $U$ the farthest. The part of the plane swept between the segments $SU$ and $S'U'$ (the initial and final positions of the line from the nearest to the farthest vertex) is $\frac18$ of an annulus with radii $OS$ and $OU$: $\frac{\pi(52-12)}{8}=5\pi$.

What remains of the swept region is, on each side of that annular part, half of the hexagon: the trapezoid $SATU$ in the starting position and the trapezoid $U'R'N'S'$ in the final position. Together these make one full hexagon, of area $6\sqrt3$.

Total area $=5\pi+6\sqrt3$. (A numerical simulation of the sweep gives $\approx 26.1$, in agreement with $5\pi+6\sqrt3\approx26.10$.)

**Answer: $5\pi+6\sqrt3$**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-07.title: Inclusion-exclusion with gcds
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-07.body:
Two moons with $m$ and $n$ full moons per month are full simultaneously exactly $\gcd(m,n)$ times per month (and all three, $\gcd(I,E,G)$ times). Let $g=\gcd(I,E,G)$. Inclusion-exclusion turns the conditions into
$$I+E+G-\gcd(I,E)-\gcd(E,G)-\gcd(I,G)+g=54,$$
$$\gcd(I,E)+\gcd(E,G)+\gcd(I,G)-2g=11.$$
Then $g$ divides both $54$ and $11$, so $g=1$. Hence the three pairwise gcds sum to $13$, and $I+E+G=54+13-1=66$.

The three pairwise gcds are pairwise coprime (the gcd of any two of them divides $g=1$), so at most one is even; their sum $13$ is odd, so none is even. The only triples of pairwise coprime odd numbers with sum $13$ are $(1,1,11)$ and $(1,5,7)$ (up to order). In the first case $11$ would divide two of $I,E,G$, hence also the third since $11\mid66$, contradicting $g=1$. So the gcds are $1,5,7$, and $I,E,G$ are $35a$, $5b$, $7c$ in some order, with $35a+5b+7c=66$ and positive integers $a,b,c$. The only solution is $a=1,b=2,c=3$, giving $\{35,10,21\}$. These do satisfy all conditions, so $IEG=35\cdot10\cdot21=7350$.

**Answer: 7350**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-08.title: Radical axis through the midpoint
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-08.body:
Let the two circumcircles meet line $SR$ again at $Y$ (circle $MXS$) and $Z$ (circle $AXR$), and let $N$ be the midpoint of $SR$. The common chord is the radical axis and passes through $N$, so $NS\cdot NY=NR\cdot NZ$ (powers of $N$). Since $NS=NR$, we get $NY=NZ$ and therefore $SY=RZ$.

Let $F_M,F_A$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $M,A$ to $SR$. Then $\sqrt{16^2-SF_M^2}=\sqrt{17^2-RF_A^2}$ (both equal the height), so $RF_A^2-SF_M^2=17^2-16^2=33$. As $SF_M+RF_A=SR-MA=11$, we get $RF_A-SF_M=3$, hence $SF_M=4$, $RF_A=7$.

$MXSY$ and $AXZR$ are cyclic with two parallel sides ($MX\parallel SY$, $AX\parallel RZ$), hence isosceles trapezoids, so $SY=MX+2\cdot SF_M=MX+8$ and $RZ=AX+2\cdot RF_A=AX+14$. From $SY=RZ$: $MX+8=AX+14$. With $MX+AX=11$ we get $MX=\tfrac{17}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{17}2$**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-08.title: Coordinates
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-08.body:
Put $S=(0,0)$, $R=(22,0)$, $M=(4,h)$, $A=(15,h)$, where $M$'s $x$-coordinate $p$ satisfies $p^2+h^2=256$ and $(p-11)^2+h^2=289$, giving $p=4$ and $h=\sqrt{240}$. For $X=(4+t,h)$ compute the powers of the midpoint $N=(11,0)$ of $SR$ with respect to the circles $MXS$ and $AXR$ and set them equal; solving for $t$ in $0<t<11$ gives $t=8.5$ (confirmed numerically), so $MX=\tfrac{17}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{17}2$**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-09.title: Always discard the rarest colour
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-09.body:
To finish, Triton must get rid of all the marbles of some colour and keep as few as possible of another. The best strategy is to always put back a marble of his *least common* colour (ties broken arbitrarily); optimality is confirmed by checking the small Markov decision process on the states (counts of the three colours up to permutation), and by a value-iteration computation which gives the same value $91/6$ from the start state $\{3,3,3\}$.

Say he works on red first. Putting a red marble in makes the bag $4$ red out of $10$. A draw is non-red with probability $\frac6{10}$, so the expected number of turns to go from $3$ to $2$ red marbles is $\frac{10}{6}$. Then the bag has $5$ red out of $10$: expected $\frac{10}{5}$ turns to go to $1$ red; then $\frac{10}{4}$ turns to remove the last red marble.

The three replacement marbles are a uniformly random $3$ of the $6$ non-red marbles from the start. There are $\binom63=20$ choices: $2$ of them give three marbles of one colour (then he has $6$ of one colour and $3$ of another and is already done), and $18$ give a split $4/5$ of the other two colours. In that case, he puts back the colour with $4$ marbles each turn and keeps whatever he draws until he draws the sixth marble of the other colour; only $1$ of the $10$ marbles in the bag is of that colour, so this takes $10$ turns in expectation.

Total expected number of turns:
$$\frac{10}{6}+\frac{10}{5}+\frac{10}{4}+\frac{18}{20}\cdot10=\frac{5}{3}+2+\frac52+9=\frac{91}{6}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{91}{6}$**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-10.title: Slopes as roots of a quadratic
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-10.body:
The two ellipses are symmetric about the origin, so the four intersection points are $\pm(x_1,y_1)$ and $\pm(x_2,y_2)$. The sides of the parallelogram have slopes $m_1=\frac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}$ and $m_2=\frac{y_1+y_2}{x_1+x_2}$.

Subtracting the two equations gives $x^2-2xy=5$ for every intersection point, and adding them gives $3x^2+2y^2=45$. Then
$$m_1+m_2=\frac{2x_1y_1-2x_2y_2}{x_1^2-x_2^2}=\frac{(x_1^2-5)-(x_2^2-5)}{x_1^2-x_2^2}=1,$$
$$m_1m_2=\frac{y_1^2-y_2^2}{x_1^2-x_2^2}=\frac12\cdot\frac{(45-3x_1^2)-(45-3x_2^2)}{x_1^2-x_2^2}=-\frac32.$$
So $m_1,m_2$ are the roots of $m^2-m-\tfrac32=0$, i.e. $m=\frac{1\pm\sqrt7}{2}$. The larger is $\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}$**

hmmt-nov-2025-thm-10.title: A pencil of conics
hmmt-nov-2025-thm-10.body:
For any $t$, every intersection point satisfies $t(x^2+xy+y^2)+(1-t)(2x^2-xy+y^2)=20t+25(1-t)$, that is $(2-t)x^2+(2t-1)xy+y^2=25-5t$. Choose $t$ so that the left side is a perfect square: the discriminant $(2t-1)^2-4(2-t)=4t^2-7$ vanishes for $t=\pm\frac{\sqrt7}2$. For each sign the left side becomes $\left(y+\frac{-1\pm\sqrt7}{2}x\right)^2$, so the four points lie on two pairs of parallel lines $y+\frac{-1\pm\sqrt7}{2}x=\text{const}$, which are the sides of the parallelogram. Their slopes are $\frac{1\mp\sqrt7}{2}$, and the largest is $\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}$ (numerically $1.8229$).

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt7}{2}$**
